Please read this carefully:

<document>
# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
# Review: Two-Year Follow-up of Varden and the Halden Subset

**Bottom line:** This is the most informative document in the series. It does what the earlier documents asked for:
- adds a log-based hours measure,
- registers the mediation test before the outcome data existed,
- reports the cost of the failed counter arm, and
- engages directly with the re-analysis and the meta-analysis.

Its rebuttal of the meta-analysis's "no decay" claim is decisive. The four long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours, which bears out the concern I raised.

The arithmetic checks out:
- Timesheet measure: 0.966 / 0.88 → +9.8%
- Log measure: 0.966 / 0.89 → +8.5%
- Halden subset: 96.8 / 86.6 → +11.8%
- Mediation shares: 47 + 18 + 35 = 100

But the report misses a problem in its own data that affects its two headline interpretations. It also says "confirms" where the design can only support "is consistent with."

## 1. The meeting audit contaminated the control group

Two of the seven control offices cut meetings in month 15 and raised output per hour by 4.1%. That improves the control group, which **biases the 24-month difference-in-differences downward**. The report presents this as an interesting aside ("an unplanned observation") but never considers its effect on the main estimates.

**Effect on the decay estimate.** If the offices are of similar size, two of seven offices gaining 4.1% raises the control average by about 1.2 points. The timesheet measure fell 2.7 points (12.5 → 9.8), so contamination could account for roughly 40% of the apparent decline. The claim that the gain "declined by about a quarter" overstates fading.

**Effect on the headline 8.5%.** The true effect of the reduced schedule, relative to an uncontaminated control, is probably somewhat higher.

**The meeting figures don't add up.** If two control offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours, the control average should have fallen by about 0.6 hours. The report says it went from 7.2 to 7.0. Either those offices are small, other control offices increased their meetings, or something is misreported. This needs reconciling.

**Possible spillover.** It is also worth asking whether the audit came from staff learning about the treated offices' meeting cuts.

The report should show the 24-month estimates with those two offices excluded, as a sensitivity analysis.

## 2. Case-processing backlogs: still not reported

The nine-month report listed "whether backlogs build up beyond the statutory deadlines" as a limitation that only follow-up could address. At 24 months it is still not addressed. There is nothing on queue length, time to decision, or the share of cases near deadline, though these sit in the same case-management system as the output data.

Output per employee has drifted from −2.1% to −3.4%. Over two years, a steady shortfall in cases closed relative to cases arriving builds up. This is the most important missing outcome. Overtime cost for case-processing is also still unreported, although the report does cost the counter arm (+9% per contact).

## 3. The mediation result is stronger than before, but not a confirmation

Registering the test before the 24-month data existed answers the analytic-flexibility part of Varga & Holm's objection. Several issues remain.

**The same offices generated and tested the hypothesis.** The meetings idea came from these seven treated offices. A pre-registered test on the same units is better than an unregistered one, but it is not an independent replication. More office-months add observations, but the number of independent units is still 14 offices. Were the confidence intervals clustered by office with a small-sample correction? A 28–66% interval looks narrow for 7 v 7 clusters.

**Confounding between mediator and outcome.** The report acknowledges this but underplays it. Managers who cut meetings may also be better managers in other ways. Meeting cuts weren't randomised, only the hours were.

**Differences in measurement error favour meetings.** Calendar data measure meeting time precisely. The fatigue scale is a noisy self-report. Measurement error attenuates a mediator's estimated share, so the comparison is tilted toward meetings. "Less than half as much" may partly reflect measurement quality, not true importance.

**What do the logs measure?** "Active log-in time on the case-management system" sounds like case work only. That changes the meaning of the meetings pathway:
- If the logs **include** meetings, cutting meetings raises output per hour almost as an accounting identity, since zero-output hours are removed from the denominator.
- If the logs **exclude** meetings, the pathway implies something behavioural, such as fewer interruptions improving case work.

These are different findings, and the report should say which one it is.

A rough check makes the point. Assume timesheet-like hours from a baseline of 37.9, meetings falling 3.3 hours relative to control, and meetings producing nothing. Then output per *non-meeting* hour is roughly flat relative to control. On that assumption, removing meeting time could account for nearly all of the per-hour gain, not 47%. Either meetings had some value, or the denominator excludes them. Either way, the decomposition needs explaining.

**Wording.** The Summary's "confirms" should be "is consistent with." The Limitations section already says as much.

## 4. The Halden subset

- **More selection.** 14 of the 23 organisations agreed to take part, on top of everything earlier. The authors label the result as an upper bound for organisations that self-selected and stayed, which is correct.
- **Survivors only.** Including the three organisations that reverted, with output of 88–91 at reversion, would give a less selective figure.
- **The marketing agency.** It reverted because of client deadlines, yet marketing would be coded "discretionary" in the meta-analysis. The Summary's phrase "client-facing or coverage obligations" stretches the category to fit. A better reading is that client responsiveness is a form of coverage, and the discretionary/coverage-bound split is fuzzier than a two-way code. That matters for anyone applying these results.
- **The Halden attrition misreporting.** R. Okafor, a Halden author, is a co-author here. The report does not acknowledge or correct the misdescribed attrition that Varga & Holm documented, namely that seven of the nine withdrawals came after the schedule began. That correction should be made formally.

## 5. Smaller points

- **Quality.** Appeal overturn rates (3.2% v 3.0%) are still raw levels, with no CI and no difference-in-differences.
- **Sick days.** The −27% may still partly reflect fewer scheduled working days.
- **Novelty.** The rebuttal of Varga & Holm on novelty is fair: the gain was still present at 24 months. However, ongoing evaluation keeps staff aware they are being observed, so a pure "being studied" effect isn't fully excluded.
- **Decline as a trend.** "Declined but not disappeared" is accurate, but two time points can't show whether the decline has stopped. The report rightly criticises the straight-line extrapolation from two energy readings, and its own two points need the same caution.

## 6. Updated picture across all six documents

| Question | Best current answer |
|---|---|
| Per-actual-hour gain, discretionary work | About +8–10% in the one randomised long follow-up; possibly somewhat higher after allowing for control contamination |
| Per-worker output, discretionary work | Slightly below control (about −3%); backlog consequences unknown |
| Coverage-bound work | Output loss confirmed; the county ended the arm, and restoring service was estimated to cost +9% per contact |
| Durability | Some decline from 9 to 24 months, overstated by contamination; beyond 24 months unknown |
| "Sector-general" (Halden) | Not supported |
| "Entirely an artifact" (Varga & Holm) | Not supported |
| "No decay" (meta-analysis) | Not supported; the long studies were all weak designs |
| Mechanism | Removing meeting time is likely a major contributor; fatigue contributes less, possibly underestimated; about a third is unexplained |
| Gains available without cutting hours? | Open; the two control offices suggest partly, but no arm tested reorganisation alone |

The last row is now the most policy-relevant open question. If meeting cuts drive much of the gain, the key comparison is *reorganisation with the hours cut* against *reorganisation alone*. The report rightly notes that it can't answer this, and the next trial should be designed around it.

## Pattern, again

This report rightly criticises the meta-analysis for drawing a decay conclusion from studies that couldn't support it. It then draws its own decay conclusion without accounting for the contamination it reported a few paragraphs later. Each document in the series has been sharpest on others' overreach and least careful with its own.

I can draft a short referee report or a consolidated evidence table across all six documents.
